blocks.instruction: Leia o texto e escolha a alternativa correta. Algumas perguntas pedem inferência — a resposta não está escrita com todas as letras.
blocks.passage:
Tone and register in British emails are subtle but critical. The same message can read as warm, neutral, or cold depending on a few small choices: the opening, the closing, the length, even the use of exclamation marks and the space between paragraphs.

A useful rule of thumb is to match the register to the relationship and the topic. A senior client on a formal proposal gets "Dear [name]", longer sentences, and "Kind regards" at the end. A regular internal colleague gets "Hi [name]", shorter lines, and "Thanks" or "Cheers". Get this wrong by one step in either direction and it feels slightly off — too stiff, or too casual.

When you are not sure, err on the side of slightly more formal. It is almost always forgiven.

items.q: According to the text, what can make the same message read as warm, neutral, or cold?
options: Small choices such as the opening, closing, and length
The subject line and the recipient's job title
The attachments included with the message
The time of day the email is sent
items.why: "a few small choices: the opening, the closing, the length…" — são esses detalhes que mudam a percepção.

items.q: What is the rule of thumb the text recommends?
options: Use the same register for every reader
Avoid exclamation marks in all emails
Match the register to the relationship and the topic
Always keep emails as short as possible
items.why: "match the register to the relationship and the topic."

items.q: What should you do when you are unsure about the register?
options: Err on the side of slightly more formal
items.why: "err on the side of slightly more formal. It is almost always forgiven."

items.q: Which statement would the author most likely DISAGREE with?
options: Register is a minor detail that rarely affects how a message lands
Being too casual can feel just as off as being too stiff
A slightly formal tone is a low-risk default
Register signals something to the reader
items.why: Inferência: o texto abre dizendo que tom e registro são "subtle but critical" — negar sua importância contraria a tese.

items.q: The phrase "by one step in either direction" suggests that…
options: both over-formality and over-casualness are mistakes
the register should change with every paragraph
erring too formal is always worse than erring too casual
only new clients notice the register
items.why: Inferência: "too stiff, or too casual" — o erro pode acontecer para qualquer um dos dois lados.

blocks.instruction: Ouça Emily orientando uma colega recém-chegada sobre o registro dos e-mails. Responda sem ler a transcrição — ela só aparece depois de corrigir.

audio.text:
Right, let's look at these three drafts together. They are all fine in content — it is the register I want to work on with you.

The first one goes to a senior client on the new proposal. Here you opened with "Hi Robert" and signed off "Cheers". That is a bit too casual for a first formal contact. I would move it up a step: "Dear Robert", full sentences, and "Kind regards" at the end. Notice I am not asking you to sound stiff — just a touch more formal.

The second one is to Sarah in operations, who you email every day. This one you made very formal, and honestly it reads a little cold. With her, "Hi Sarah", a shorter line or two, and "Thanks" is perfect. Save the long sentences for the client.

And the third, to the wider team, sits nicely in the middle. That one I would leave as it is.

My rule, when you are not sure which way to go, is simple: pick one level more formal than you think you need. Nobody has ever complained that an email was too polite.
audio.label: Ouça quantas vezes precisar. A transcrição aparece depois de corrigir.

items.q: What does Emily say is fine about all three drafts?
items.why: "They are all fine in content — it is the register I want to work on."

items.q: What is wrong with the first draft, sent to a senior client?
options: It opens with "Hi Robert" and signs off "Cheers" — too casual
It uses no greeting at all
It is too long and detailed
It has too many exclamation marks
items.why: "you opened with 'Hi Robert' and signed off 'Cheers'. That is a bit too casual."

items.q: Why does Emily want the second email, to Sarah, changed?
options: It is very formal and reads a little cold
items.why: "you made very formal, and honestly it reads a little cold" — com uma colega diária, algo mais leve cabe melhor.

items.q: What does Emily mean when she says the email to Sarah 'reads a little cold'?
options: The email is too long to read quickly
The tone feels distant given how close the working relationship is
The email was sent to the wrong person
items.why: Inferência: um registro formal demais entre pessoas que se falam todo dia soa distante, não profissional.

items.q: What is Emily's overall advice when someone is unsure of the register?
options: Go one level more formal than you think you need
Copy the tone of the last email received
Always keep it neutral and in the middle
items.why: "pick one level more formal than you think you need. Nobody has ever complained that an email was too polite."

blocks.instruction: O vocabulário da lição aparece aqui em frases novas. Escolha o sentido ou a palavra que cabe no contexto.

items.q: "The email was technically correct, but the register was wrong for a first client contact." Register here means…
options: the subject line of the message
the level of formality of the language
the record of who was copied in
items.why: Register = registro: o nível de formalidade da linguagem.

items.q: Choose the correct phrase: "A useful ___ is to match the register to the reader."
items.why: Rule of thumb = regra prática, um princípio geral e fácil de lembrar.

items.q: "The proposal read as too stiff for someone she speaks to every day." Stiff here means…
items.why: Stiff = engessado, formal e rígido demais para o contexto.

items.q: Choose the correct phrase: "When you are unsure, ___ slightly more formal — it is almost always forgiven."
items.why: Err on the side of = pender para o lado de (a opção mais segura).

items.q: "Using three exclamation marks in a client email can undercut your credibility." An exclamation mark is…
options: the greeting at the top of an email
the '!' punctuation used to add emphasis
items.why: Exclamation mark = ponto de exclamação, o sinal '!'.

blocks.instruction: Expressões e phrasal verbs comuns quando se fala de e-mails e comunicação profissional. Escolha o sentido no contexto.

items.q: "Can you run this past Emily before you send it to the client?" To run something past someone means to…
options: show it to them for a quick opinion
items.why: Run past = mostrar a alguém para ter uma opinião ou aval rápido.

items.q: "Her tone was warm, but she still managed to get her point across." This means she…
items.why: Get your point across = conseguir transmitir a mensagem com clareza.

items.q: "Let me tone down the exclamation marks before this goes out." To tone something down means to…
options: make it less intense or extreme
items.why: Tone down = suavizar, deixar menos intenso.

items.q: "The client's reply felt cold, but I do not want to read too much into it." This means she does not want to…
options: assume more meaning than is really there
reply to the message at all
items.why: Read too much into = atribuir mais significado do que realmente existe.

items.q: "A polished, well-judged email really goes a long way with British clients." This means it…
options: has a large and positive effect
takes a long time to write
items.why: Goes a long way = faz muita diferença, tem um efeito grande e positivo.
